question:
A 48-year-old male rower presents with a 6-month history of progressive burning pain and paresthesia
affecting his right medial thigh. The symptoms are persistent and worsen with rowing activities and
prolonged sitting in his compact sports car. The pain is limited to above the knee, and he reports no
sensory deficits. There is no history of trauma or injury, and physical therapy has been ineffective.
Physical examination reveals normal hip range of motion and a negative FABER test. Straight-leg-raise
test is negative, and lower extremity reflexes are symmetrical. Muscle strength testing shows slight
weakness in right hip adduction. Hip radiographs demonstrate no abnormalities. What is the most
probable diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) Adductor muscle strain (B) Meralgia paresthetica (C) Hip
labral tear (D) L2–3 nerve-root compression (E) S1 nerve-root compression (F) Obturator nerve
entrapment (G) Sacroiliac joint dysfunction (H) Femoral nerve compression (I) Lumbar facet syndrome
(J) Iliopsoas tendinitis
 A. Hip labral tear
B. Lumbar facet syndrome
C. Adductor muscle strain
D. Obturator nerve entrapment
E. Femoral nerve compression
F. Meralgia paresthetica
G. Iliopsoas tendinitis
H. L2–3 nerve-root compression
I. Sacroiliac joint dysfunction
J. S1 nerve-root compression
